cards.title: Set and scale Google Ads campaign budgets safely
cards.summary: Understand average daily budget vs total spend, ignore unreliable forecasts, and scale in controlled increments.
cards.use_when: Launching a new Google Ads search campaign or increasing budget on an existing one.
steps: Enter an average daily budget — the amount Google can spend per day on average, not a lifetime cap that stops the campaign once exhausted.
Treat Google's conversion, conversion value and cost-per-conversion forecasts as unreliable, especially when starting out; do not build spend decisions on them.
Start only with a budget you are comfortable losing entirely, since early performance is volatile.
Scale gradually rather than doubling or tripling overnight: the source suggests moving from $50/day to $60, then $70, then $100.
Remember every setting (budget, bidding, keywords) can be changed at any point during the campaign's life.
Expect delayed serving and volatile, sometimes very expensive initial clicks while Google learns; wait up to a day before troubleshooting.
If no serving occurs beyond one to two days, check bidding setup and whether keywords have enough search volume.
caveats: The $50→$100 example is the source's illustrative path, not a benchmark; choose increments based on your own margins.
Google's budget forecasts are described as 'vastly inaccurate' — verify performance with your own data.

cards.title: Choose keyword match types by account maturity and goal
cards.summary: Match type selection depends on conversion data and whether you prioritize efficiency or growth.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to add exact, phrase or broad keywords to a search campaign.
steps: Understand the three types: broad match (no notation) casts the widest net; phrase match (quotation marks) is moderate; exact match (square brackets) is tightest, requiring near-identical meaning or intent.
If your account is new, has little conversion data, or you prioritize efficiency, lead with exact match keywords you know convert (e.g. from Amazon or previous tests) to avoid wasted spend.
If you are growth-focused and have substantial conversion data, lean into broad match, which pairs well with automated bid strategies like Maximize Conversion Value or Target ROAS.
For a middle-ground approach the source suggests roughly 80% exact match plus core broad-match keywords, using broad to surface new converting search terms that you later promote to exact.
Note that the source's team is using phrase match less because it has become broader in behavior.
caveats: The '80% exact' split is the source's heuristic, not a calculated rule.
All match types are trending broader as Google shifts away from manual keyword control; re-verify current behavior in the interface.

cards.title: Classify keywords into four funnel types before targeting
cards.summary: Informational, commercial, transactional and navigational keywords require different landing destinations.
cards.use_when: Planning keyword lists and choosing where each keyword's traffic should land.
steps: Informational (top of funnel, e.g. 'how to take collagen for best results'): users want education, not purchase — send to an advertorial-style landing page or blog, not a PDP.
Commercial (mid funnel, e.g. 'best collagen powder for women over 50' or competitor comparisons): users are comparing; bucket with transactional keywords under 'performance search'.
Transactional (mid-to-bottom funnel, e.g. 'buy collagen powder for women over 50'): imperative verbs signal near-purchase; route to purchase-ready pages.
Navigational (bottom funnel, mostly branded, e.g. '[brand] collagen reviews' or promo-code searches): send to a reviews page, promo page, or the specific product page.
Concentrate keyword research effort on commercial and transactional terms, since that is where most advertisers compete and where better research has the biggest impact.
caveats: Sending informational traffic straight to a product page is ineffective because intent does not match, per the source.

cards.title: Run the seed-expand-segment keyword research method
cards.summary: Build 20-30 seed keywords, expand each into long-tail variants, then segment by theme into ad groups.
cards.use_when: Building or rebuilding a search campaign keyword list for a DTC product.
steps: Find 20-30 seed keywords: two-to-three-word phrases identifying your core product (e.g. 'collagen', "women's collagen", 'marine collagen').

Expand each seed into long-tail keywords mirroring how users now search (e.g. from 'women's collagen': 'best collagen for women', "women's collagen for joint support", 'best collagen for women over 50', 'tasty collagen for women').
Validate candidates in Google Keyword Planner for search volume, 3-month and year-on-year change, competition, and low/high top-of-page bid ranges.
Estimate likely conversion rate from historical paid traffic and store data; if the CPC, conversion rate and target CAC/ROAS numbers don't work, exclude the keyword initially.

Segment surviving keywords into themed ad groups (e.g. women over 50, joint support, flavor, flavorless, peptides, hair growth, collagen with vitamin C) so ad copy and landing pages stay tightly aligned.
Expect to reduce hundreds of long-tail candidates down to roughly 20-25 to target initially.
caveats: Keyword Planner bids and volumes are directional, not exact.
The 20-30 seeds and 20-25 final keywords are the source's working ranges, not fixed thresholds.

cards.title: Use Keyword Planner, Semrush and ChatGPT for keyword ideation
cards.summary: Three complementary sources for finding long-tail keyword candidates.
cards.use_when: Generating more long-tail keyword ideas after you've defined your seed keywords.
steps: Use Google Keyword Planner for volume, 3-month and year-on-year trend, competition level, and low/high top-of-page bid estimates.
Use Semrush (paid) for keyword ideation and research — the source recommends it as a long-standing tool but notes it isn't required.
Give ChatGPT your seed keywords and ask it to generate additional long-tail variations once Planner and Semrush ideas run out; it's good at exhaustive long-tail lists.
Identify and define the core seed keywords yourself rather than relying on ChatGPT for that step.
Combine all sources, then filter against CPC, competition, expected conversion rate and target CAC/ROAS before loading anything into campaigns.
caveats: Semrush is optional; Google Ads plus ChatGPT can work for low-budget accounts.
ChatGPT output duplicates and inaccuracies are common — validate against Keyword Planner.

cards.title: Apply negative keyword match types correctly
cards.summary: Broad, phrase and exact negative keywords block different amounts of traffic — choose deliberately.
cards.use_when: Filtering irrelevant search terms out of a search or shopping campaign to cut wasted spend.
steps: Broad negative (plain term, e.g. running shoes): blocks searches containing all terms in any order; e.g. 'blue running shoes' and 'shoes running' blocked, but 'blue tennis shoes' (missing 'running') and 'running shoe' (singular) may still show.

Phrase negative (quotation marks): blocks searches containing the exact terms in the same order with other words allowed around them; 'blue running shoes' blocked, but 'shoes running' (wrong order) may show.
Exact negative (square brackets): the tightest — blocks only searches matching the exact terms in the same order with no extra words; almost everything else may still show.
Use broad negatives where a single variant represents a clear category you never want (e.g. a competitor or a different product type); use exact when you only want to exclude a specific query.
Note that all three negative types apply, and match-type logic mirrors positive keywords.
caveats: Singular/plural differences (shoe vs shoes) affect blocking — spell out variants you need to exclude.
Broad negatives can accidentally block valuable long-tail queries if not chosen carefully.

cards.title: Choose negative keyword level and review cadence
cards.summary: Apply negatives at account, campaign or ad-group level and review search term reports frequently while accounts are new.
cards.use_when: Setting up a negative keyword structure or deciding how often to review search term reports.
steps: Add negatives individually (when you spot a bad search term in the report) or as a negative keyword list you can apply in bulk.
Apply at ad group level for tightest control; at campaign level to affect all ad groups in one campaign; at account level to affect all existing and future campaigns.
Note the hierarchy: account negatives affect everything, campaign negatives affect that campaign's ad groups, ad group negatives affect only that ad group.
Review search term reports daily in new accounts or while testing new keywords/products, adding negatives immediately to save money from day one.
Reduce to a couple of times per week once performance is stable and search terms are cleaner — sometimes no additions will be needed.
caveats: Account-level negatives persist into new campaigns, so use them sparingly or they will apply invisible constraints across everything.
Daily review is most valuable early; frequency should flex with search volume and account maturity.

cards.title: Use quality score to understand ad rank and CPC
cards.summary: Quality score (1-10) drives ad rank and CPC via expected CTR, ad relevance and landing page experience.
cards.use_when: Diagnosing why the same keyword costs far more than competitors or planning account improvements.
steps: Understand ad rank: on each search, Google rates eligible ads and serves higher-ranked ones in better positions.
Recognize the bid is only one ad-rank input; improving ad quality is usually cheaper than raising bids to climb positions.

Assess quality score's three components: expected click-through rate (vs competitors), ad relevance (does the ad match query and intent), and landing page experience (load speed, responsiveness, relevance, conversion).
Check components in the keyword view — a keyword scoring 3 can have below-average expected CTR while ad relevance and landing page experience are average; fix the weakest first.

Note that a single keyword's average CPC was reduced from $5.84 to $2.38 (per the source) through ad and landing page tweaks, illustrating that quality score directly affects unit economics and scalability.
caveats: The $5.84→$2.38 example is a source example, not a guaranteed outcome; results depend on the keyword and account.
Quality score components are relative to other advertisers, so they change even when you aren't making edits.

cards.title: Improve quality score via three levers
cards.summary: Concrete actions to raise expected CTR, ad relevance and landing page experience.
cards.use_when: Working on a low quality score keyword or preparing a new search campaign for competitive terms.
steps: For expected CTR: strengthen headlines; match user intent — don't serve a 'best collagen' ad to someone researching 'benefits of collagen powder' at the top of the funnel.
Add relevant ad extensions (sitelinks, callouts) to give users more information and more reasons to click.
Continuously test headline angles — expected CTR is relative and non-static, so standing still while competitors test means your score declines.
For ad relevance: segment ad groups by intent/theme so ad copy can address one user need; use dynamic keyword insertion so the actual search query appears in the headline or description.
Match the user's language — use problem-aware phrasing for problem-aware queries, not technical jargon the searcher may not know.

For landing page experience: improve load times (use PageSpeed Insights), match landing page headlines to ad headlines and search queries, provide clear CTAs and a frictionless conversion path, and optimize for mobile.
caveats: Landing page experience includes whether the page converts well (per the source), not just speed and match.
Dynamic keyword insertion requires careful capitalization/fallback setup to avoid awkward renderings.

cards.title: Build single theme asset groups (STAGs) instead of mixed ad groups
cards.summary: Tightly themed ad groups keep keyword, ad copy and landing page congruent, raising quality score and lowering CPC.
cards.use_when: Restructuring an existing search campaign or building a new one where keywords have divergent intents.
steps: Replace messy ad groups containing mixed intents (e.g. 'buy running shoes', 'cheap gym trainers', 'shoes for plantar fasciitis', 'running shoes for women') with single-theme groups like general running shoes, bargain hunters, plantar fasciitis, ladies trainers.
Within each theme, align keywords, ad copy and landing page so a user searching a plantar-fasciitis term sees plantar-fasciitis language in the ad and lands on a page addressing that need.
Expect STAGs to lift all three quality score components: higher CTR from tighter matching, higher ad relevance, and better landing page experience (longer dwell, fewer bounces, more conversions).
Segment further where intents diverge — the source says not all keywords in a suggested theme must sit in one ad group if intent differs.
This replaces the older SCAG (single keyword ad group) approach the source used in 2018-2019.
caveats: More granular ad groups mean more management overhead; the source accepts this tradeoff for the relevance gain.
The lift described is the source's observed mechanism, not a guaranteed outcome for every account.

cards.title: Size ad groups with 2-8 keywords to preserve relevance
cards.summary: Keep each ad group to a handful of closely related keywords rather than stuffing in dissimilar terms.
cards.use_when: Segmenting keyword lists into ad groups for a search campaign.
steps: Place two to three keywords per ad group, and up to about five to eight.
When adding a keyword that doesn't fit the ad group's theme, create a new ad group instead of forcing it in.
Er on the side of breaking things out rather than bundling — the source repeatedly prefers more granular segmentation to protect keyword/ad/landing page alignment.
Recheck segmentation whenever you add a new keyword found via search term reports or broad-match expansion.
caveats: The 2-3 to 5-8 range is the source's working heuristic, not a fixed rule.
Very granular structures require more ad copy and landing page variation to maintain the benefit.

cards.title: Write headlines that grab, match intent and drive action
cards.summary: Headlines (30 characters) should hook, match the query and include a CTA, using specific formatting conventions.
cards.use_when: Writing or testing RSA headlines for a search campaign.
steps: Ensure each headline does one of three jobs: grab attention with an emotional hook or benefit, match user intent by including target keywords where possible, or guide action with a clear imperative verb (Shop, Buy, Explore, Learn).
Use title case for readability (e.g. 'Shop The Collection').
Use numbers and symbols to stand out on a noisy SERP — e.g. inseam lengths like 5", 7.5", 9", or a '#' symbol for 'number one'.
Use 'you' and 'your' to speak directly to the searcher (e.g. 'Your New Favorite Shorts').
Reflect positive outcomes that matter to your customer (e.g. 'Burn Fat And Glow').
Show off your offer in a headline when it is strong — e.g. a free trial or a limited-time bundle discount — since offers increase clickability.
caveats: Headlines match user intent by including target keywords, but don't force irrelevance — a 'best collagen' headline wastes money for a searcher researching benefits.
Offer headlines assume a genuinely strong offer; weak offers won't rescue click-through.

cards.title: Write descriptions to close, handle objections and build trust
cards.summary: Use the 90-character descriptions to elaborate, reduce risk and add urgency or proof.
cards.use_when: Drafting RSA descriptions for a search campaign.
steps: Treat descriptions as the closer — their job is handling objections, reinforcing value, adding urgency and providing trust signals before the click.
Use a problem-solution format, optionally drawn from a customer review to add credibility (e.g. 'Our dog had the worst breath and this is the only product that has worked').
Use an offer-deadline format to create urgency (e.g. 'Hurry before they're gone. Get yours with monthly toys and treats').
Use a benefit + trust signal format (e.g. 'Skin-loving ultra gentle close shave, dermatologist approved for sensitive skin').
Remember two descriptions can serve at once and each is up to 90 characters, so pair formats that don't duplicate each other.
caveats: The example formats are observed from competitor accounts; test which format your audience responds to rather than assuming one wins.

cards.title: Avoid maxing out and pinning RSA assets
cards.summary: Limit headlines and avoid pinning unless you have a specific reason, to preserve learning and testing.
cards.use_when: Building or revising a responsive search ad.
steps: Don't max out 15 headlines for the sake of it — the source typically uses seven to eight or nine so that individual asset performance is not diluted across traffic.
Ensure headlines vary meaningfully because two or three serve together; do not use near-identical headline variants.
Test headline angles continuously; once you have seven to nine headlines, click-through feedback on what works arrives relatively quickly.
Pin headlines or descriptions only when you have a specific reason: a promotion that must always show, or an angle with proven high CTR. Otherwise let Google rotate assets.
Treat Google's 'ad strength' indicator as separate from ad rank; don't fill every slot just to satisfy ad strength.
Add more headlines only if you have genuinely distinct viable angles that need testing.
caveats: Google's own interface recommends filling more assets; the source disagrees in the interest of clean test read-outs.
Pinning a promotion ensures delivery but reduces the rotation freedom of other assets.
